name: Blackfoot, Siksika dialect

catalog_citation: Van Der Mark, Sheena Chantal. 2003. The phonetics of Blackfoot pitch accent. MA thesis, University of Calgary. xiii+113 pp. Open PDF: https://hdl.handle.net/1880/40174 (ucalgary.scholaris.ca).
catalog_locator: §2.2.5 'Pitch accent', pp. 11-12 (PDF pp. 24-25 of the copy we hold; text layer the copy we ll. 975-1000)
catalog_quote: Blackfoot PA is primarily lexical. Blackfoot words typically contain one pitch accent; no words are accentless, while some words contain more than one PA. However, multiple PAs uncommon, occurring in a few types of poly-morphemic words such as compounds or verb complexes. A PA can occur on either a long or short vowel. Additionally, Blackfoot has a small number of contour PAs - both rising and falling. These occur only on long vowels, with the PA associated with only one mora; the first for falling PAs, and the second for rising PAs. Syllable weight appears to interact with PA in Blackfoot, though not consistently. Kaneko (1999) notes that PA tends to fall of heavy syllables. While there are numerous exceptions to this generalization, it appears to be an active component of the Siksika grammar in that other phonological changes fall from this fact.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Siksika/Blackfoot is not in the catalog. Two title hits: Van Der Mark 2003 (MA thesis, already held by the project from the earlier reading) is squarely about word-level pitch accent and states it is primarily lexical, one accent per word, with an inconsistent preference for heavy syllables (§2.2.5 pp. 11-12); Both and. Best first-hand statement: Van Der Mark 2003 §2.2.5, corroborated by Stacy 2004, Elfner 2006, Frantz 1970, Uhlenbeck 1938 and the Van der Mark 2002 summary of Kaneko 1999 (heavy syllable takes accent; leftmost heavy if several; lexical when all light). Still unread and worth acquiring for a fuller rule: Kaneko 1999 (UBC MA), Frantz 1991/2009 Blackfoot Grammar (pp. 3, 34), Taylor 1969 (p. 25), Weber 2020 (UBC PhD). all access went through DOI/API/automated download.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Blackfoot is a pitch accent language: each word normally carries one lexically specified high-pitch accent (marked with an acute in Frantz's orthography) whose position is not predictable from syllable count or word edge; it may fall on a long or short vowel anywhere in the word. Tendencies reported but not rules: accent prefers heavy syllables (leftmost heavy in monomorphemic nouns, Kaneko 1999 via Van der Mark 2002:181), often sits near the left edge and avoids the right edge (Stacy 2004). Elfner 2006:14 sums up: 'accent placement in Blackfoot is virtually unpredictable, although some generalisations exist'. Frantz 1991:34, 65 (via Stacy) says the accent-assignment rules are 'poorly understood'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress in the modern accounts (culminative single PA; extra PAs in compounds are treated as multiple accents, not secondary). Uhlenbeck 1938:9-10 marks a 'secondary stress or stresses' with the grave in Southern Peigan, and says it is often impossible to decide which stress is strongest.
new_statements.exceptions: Multiple PAs in some compounds and verb complexes; contour (rising/falling) PAs on long vowels linked to one mora; weight tendency has 'numerous exceptions'. Stacy 2004:11-12, 75: ~10% of imperatives take a discourse-driven accent on the stem-final vowel; devoiced ('deficient') syllables and right-edge elements do not bear accent; some polymorphemic words surface with no accent or with adjacent accents. Uhlenbeck 1938:9 (Southern Peigan) reports 'wavering stress' and disyllables with equal stress on both syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: elicited citation forms of nouns and verbs from five Siksika-dialect speakers (ch. 5, p. 35). Frantz 1991:3 (quoted in Stacy 2004:55) notes utterance-level declination, so a late accented syllable may be lower in absolute pitch than an earlier unaccented one but remains high relative to the following syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: siks1238 is the language-level code for Blackfoot/Blackfeet (Siksika, Kainai/Blood, Piikani/Peigan, Aamsskaapipikani/South Peigan dialects). The quoted statement (Van Der Mark 2003) describes the Siksika dialect specifically (five Siksika Nation speakers, Alberta); Kaneko 1999's weight generalisations come from Blood (Kainai) speakers; Uhlenbeck 1938's expiratory-stress description is Southern Peigan (Montana, 1910s data). Frantz 1991 covers Blackfoot generally. All sources treat the accent system as shared across dialects.

new_statements.reading: Blackfoot (Siksika) word prominence is a lexically specified pitch accent, culminative in the sense that every word carries at least one accent, with a weak weight attraction (heavy syllables preferred, many exceptions). No fixed positional stress rule. Corroborated first-hand by Stacy 2004 §2.3.4 pp. 11-12 ('Accent is mainly lexical in Blackfoot'; prominence avoids the right edge of the word; Taylor 1969:25 said any syllable can be stressed), by Elfner 2006 §2.3.3 p. 14 ('accent placement in Blackfoot is virtually unpredictable'), by Frantz 1970 ('word stress patterns appear to be a function of both vowel length and inherent stress of certain syllables'), and by Uhlenbeck 1938 §5 pp. 9-10 (one or more expiratory accents per word, position varies, 'wavering stress'). Van der Mark 2002:181 summarises Kaneko 1999's nominal rule: a single heavy syllable takes the accent, leftmost heavy if several, lexical if all light. Suggested coding: lexical/unpredictable accent (pitch accent type), weight-sensitive tendency.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prominence is marked primarily by pitch. Its position is not given by a fixed rule: it depends partly on vowel length (heavy syllables attract it) and partly on 'inherent' (lexically marked) stress of particular syllables, with the rules apparently also sensitive to whether the word is a verb or a noun; Frantz says the analysis of the system was incomplete.
new_statements.exceptions: No fixed rule is offered, so no exceptions are listed; the noun/verb minimal pair nitomitaama 'my dog' vs nitomitaami 'I have a dog' is given to show that stress rules must see nominal vs verbal status.
new_statements.identity_note: Frantz 1970/1971: data principally from the Blackfoot (Siksika) Reserve, Alberta, plus one Montana Blackfeet consultant. Miyashita & Fish 2015: a single elderly male Blackfeet (Amsskaapipiikani, Montana) speaker, Chief Earl Old Person; not Siksika. Weber 2020, Weber & Allen 2012, Prins 2019 and Tailfeathers 1993 were not opened, so their varieties are unverified (Prins and Weber are known to work mostly with Blackfeet/Kainai speakers, but that is not from the texts).

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's lexical pitch accent reading (at least one accent per word, position lexical/unpredictable, weight-sensitivity claimed by Kaneko) and refines it with (a) a first-three-syllables observation for short words, (b) Taylor 1969's two impressionistic contour types (Type I: prominent syllable near the beginning, high-pitched; Type II: final or penultimate, high intensity but low, steady pitch), and (c) the note that the predictability question is contested. The data are from a Blackfeet (Amsskaapipiikani, Montana) speaker, not Siksika; the slides treat Blackfoot as one language.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Blackfoot has a lexical pitch accent realised as high F0; every word has at least one accented syllable. The slides restate the older view that the accent's position is unpredictable (Uhlenbeck 1938, Frantz 2009) and note that Kaneko 1999 (quantity-sensitive, culminativity, alignment) and Weber (iambic feet) claim it is largely predictable, with frequent words as counterexamples. In their own measurements of 35 two-, three- and four-syllable words from one elderly Blackfeet speaker (Chief Earl Old Person), the highest-F0 syllable was the first, second or third, never the fourth; accented syllables are higher word-initially and downdrift; long accented vowels rise toward the end or drop in the middle.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated; 'Words with multiple accents' is listed under future work (slide 38).
new_statements.exceptions: Frequent words (boy, man, baby) are counterexamples to the predictability accounts; the data set is 35 words in isolation from a single speaker, so 'first, second or third syllable' is an observation, not a rule.

readall_conflicts: The one live disagreement in the literature, restated by Miyashita & Fish 2015 slide 9, is whether accent position is predictable: Uhlenbeck 1938 and Frantz 2009 (and Frantz 1970, 'analysis of this system is still incomplete') treat it as lexical/unpredictable, while Kaneko 1999 (quantity-sensitive, culminativity and alignment) and Weber (iambic feet; the 2020 dissertation and the 2012 Weber & Allen paper could not be opened) claim it is largely predictable, with frequent words (boy, man, baby) as counterexamples. our earlier reading's note that Stacy 2004 rejects the pitch accent label in favour of a tonal analysis stands; nothing opened here bears on it.

sources.quote: Blackfoot orthographic convention (Frantz 1978) is to write pitch accented vowels with accents. Long vowels and consonants, which are contrastive (Frantz 1978; 2009; Frantz & Russell 1995; Elfner 2006), are written as double letters. [p. 1 fn. 1] ... it is possible to analyze the plural morpheme -iksi as being a sequence of syllables, possibly a metrical foot. However, because this suffix does not appear to contribute stress to any of the tokens analyzed, there is no reason to assume a metrical foot is the correct analysis of this structure. [p. 11]
sources.note: Paper is about prosodic constituency (syllable vs prosodic word vs phonological phrase), diagnosed by vowel coalescence and right-edge aspiration, and its mapping to morphosyntactic categories. It contains no statement of where word-level pitch accent/stress falls; the only accent remarks are the orthographic footnote and the aside that the plural suffix -iksi bears no stress in the tokens analysed.

sources.access_detail: bibliographic record only
sources.note: archive.org copy (blackfootgrammar0000fran) is lending-restricted, Google Books preview blocked (not reachable by automated download), so not opened. Second-hand via Stacy 2004:55-56: Frantz 1991:3 'prominence.. consists primarily of a relatively higher pitch than that of contiguous syllables'; 1991:34, 65 'accent assignment rules [are] poorly understood' / 'not yet fully understood by this investigator'; 1991:34 PA is 'sensitive to' syllable structure; accented syllable late in a word may be absolutely lower in pitch because of declination but is still high relative to the following syllable.
